source: PaperBench: Starace et al. (2025)
finding: Agents must replicate 20 ICML 2024 papers from scratch, graded by 8,316 rubric items. Best agent scored low.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new) with BasicAgent 21.0% (SEM 0.8); o1-high 13.2%; DeepSeek-R1 6.0%; Gemini 2.0 Flash 3.2%; 3 runs per paper, 12 h limit.
limits: Only 20 papers; Claude 3.7 not run (rate limits).
agent_relevance: A replication score is partial credit over many checks; a single pass/fail hides how far the agent got.

source: PaperBench: Starace et al. (2025)
finding: Prompt scaffold changed results a lot and in different directions per model. IterativeAgent forbids ending early and asks for piecemeal work.
numbers: IterativeAgent: o1-high 24.4%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 16.1% (down from 21.0%), o3-mini-high 8.5%. o1 with 36 h limit: 26.0%.
limits: Prompt tuned for o-series; authors suspect a no-early-stop Claude variant would beat o1.
agent_relevance: Scaffold effects are model-specific. Test any loop change per model, do not assume it transfers.

source: PaperBench: Starace et al. (2025)
finding: Models stopped early, claimed success, and did not plan around the time limit. They write plans but do not carry them out.
numbers: All models except Claude 3.5 Sonnet 'frequently finished early'. o1 score plateaus after the first hour.
limits: Log inspection of several runs, not systematic counts.
agent_relevance: Add a forced check that claimed work was really run (G3, G6); do not trust 'done' claims.

source: PaperBench: Starace et al. (2025)
finding: Human baseline: 8 ML PhDs, best of 3 attempts per paper, small paper subset. Humans were slow at first but won after 24 h.
numbers: Human best@3 41.4% on the 3-paper subset vs best agent about 26% (o1, extended). o1 led early and fell behind after 24 h.
limits: Small N; humans part-time over 4 weeks; some had an A100.
agent_relevance: Agents front-load output then plateau. A second-look stage is where humans gain.

source: PaperBench: Starace et al. (2025)
finding: LLM judge used to grade replication against a rubric agreed well with human graders.
numbers: Best judge (o3-mini-high with custom scaffold) F1 0.83 on auxiliary evaluation; Code-Dev variant: o1 43.4%.
limits: Judge tested on a limited gold set.
agent_relevance: An LLM checker with a fixed rubric is a workable G3 check when the rubric is written first.

source: CORE-Bench: Siegel et al. (2024, v2 2026)
finding: Computational reproducibility benchmark: run a paper's code in a CodeOcean capsule and answer questions. Hard level has no run instructions.
numbers: CORE-Agent (AutoGPT plus task hints) with GPT-4o: 60.00% Easy, 57.78% Medium, 21.48% Hard (pass@1, test set).
limits: GPT-4o-mini scored lower; AutoGPT run once for cost.
agent_relevance: Task-specific hints lifted a general agent a lot; even then the hard level stays under a quarter.

source: CORE-Bench: Siegel et al. (2024, v2 2026)
finding: Table 1 gathers human computational-reproducibility audits across fields: many studies fail even with code and data.
numbers: Examples: Pérignon 2024 finance 484 of 1008; Trisovic 2022 1480 of 2000; Hardwicke 2021 psychology 16 of 25; Gertler 2018 economics 128 of 203; Stockemer 2018 political science 21 of 71; Collberg 2016 CS 311 of 601; ML challenge 2022: 18 of 28 fully reproducible, 6 of 28 not even after asking the authors.
limits: Column header garbled in text extraction; the second number may be the count reproduced, check the original table before citing.
agent_relevance: Base rate: even correct code often fails to rerun. An agent should expect a re-run can fail for environment reasons, not only wrong ideas.

source: REPRO-Bench: Hu et al. (2025)
finding: Agents must score the reproducibility (1 to 4) of 112 social science papers from the paper PDF plus reproduction package.
numbers: gpt-4o agents: AutoGPT 20.5%, CORE-Agent 21.4% (below 25% chance), SWE-Agent 1.8% (10.7% adjusted). Cost about $2 per task.
limits: Single base model (gpt-4o); applicability only 46 to 61% for AutoGPT and CORE-Agent.
agent_relevance: Judging whether a result holds is harder than rerunning code; agents often fail to find files.

source: REPRO-Bench: Hu et al. (2025)
finding: REPRO-AGENT adds three prompt changes: a success-case template, a dummy fallback score written first, and common error sources as few-shot hints.
numbers: Accuracy 36.6% vs 21.4% for CORE-Agent (+71% relative); applicability 92.9% vs 60.7% (+53%).
limits: Tuned on the same benchmark failure types (Stata logs, path issues); may not transfer.
agent_relevance: A write-a-fallback-first step and failure-mode hints are cheap scaffold ideas with measured gain.

source: Kohler et al. (2026) Read the Paper, Write the Code
finding: Agents reimplement analyses from the paper's methods text and the data only, never seeing code or results. 48 papers with human-verified reproducibility.
numbers: Coefficient sign agrees 75% (SWE-Agent GPT-5.4) to 91% (OpenCode GPT-5.4); naive 'always positive' gets 68%. Best agent within 1.96 original SE over 80% of the time. Four scaffolds x four LLMs.
limits: Pre-cutoff vs post-cutoff papers showed no significant difference in a small sample; leakage not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Information isolation (no sight of target numbers) is a design for honest G3 checks.

source: Kohler et al. (2026) Read the Paper, Write the Code
finding: Scaffold and model interact strongly. Failures come mostly from papers that under-specify methods, less from agent mistakes.
numbers: GPT-5.4 on OpenCode beat GPT-5.4 on Codex CLI and mini-SWE-Agent; better score linked to much higher token use. For the strongest agents, agent errors were a minor share of gaps.
limits: Error attribution itself done by an LLM, with an audit.
agent_relevance: Hidden choices in a method description decide the result. Our agent should record every analytic choice it makes.

source: Kohler et al. (2026) Read the Paper, Write the Code
finding: Cell-level grading: sign match, then relative-difference bands A to F, and an LLM traces each gap to a root cause.
numbers: Grades: A 0 to 2% difference, B 2 to 20%, C 20 to 40%, D 40 to 60%, E 60%+ or wrong sign, F missing.
limits: Grading scheme is the authors' choice.
agent_relevance: Graded closeness beats pass/fail for tracking progress in a verify loop.

source: Baumann et al. (2025) Large Language Model Hacking
finding: Config choices (model, prompt wording) in LLM annotation change statistical conclusions. 37 tasks from 21 social science papers, 18 LLMs, 13 million labels, 2,361 hypotheses.
numbers: Wrong conclusion in about 31% of hypotheses for top models and about 50% for small models. Type II errors 31 to 59%. Reversed sign in 4 to 16% of cases.
limits: Risk metric averages Type I, II and S errors; simulation over tested configs, not a universal rate.
agent_relevance: An LLM used as an instrument has researcher degrees of freedom. Fix the config before looking at results.

source: Baumann et al. (2025) Large Language Model Hacking
finding: Intentional hacking is easy: trying a handful of prompt paraphrases across models finds any desired result.
numbers: False positive achievable for 94.4% of null hypotheses; true effect hidden in 98.1%; significant effect reversed in 68.3% of true-effect cases.
limits: Upper bound: assumes the analyst picks the best model-prompt combination after seeing results.
agent_relevance: This is p-hacking by prompt. Rule: do not choose among prompts after seeing the answer (G3).

source: Baumann et al. (2025) Large Language Model Hacking
finding: What predicts error: nearness to p=0.05 matters most; prompt engineering matters least; inter-annotator agreement does not predict risk.
numbers: Error near p of 0.05 approaches 70%. Task traits explain 21% of variance, model performance 8%, prompt choices under 1%. Only 2.7% of correct significant effects had magnitude within 10% of truth (GPT-4o).
limits: Variance shares are not causal (authors say so).
agent_relevance: Borderline results from LLM steps need extra verification; careful wording will not fix it.

source: Baumann et al. (2025) Large Language Model Hacking
finding: Mitigation: human labels beat more LLM labels. Regression correction fixes false positives but raises false negatives.
numbers: 100 human annotations give Type I about 10% vs 30 to 40% for uncorrected hybrid; 1,000 human labels reduce overall risk to about 20% (from 31 to 50%); DSL and CDI correction raise Type II by up to 60 points.
limits: Based on the tested hypothesis set.
agent_relevance: A small trusted check set beats scaling up the model's own labels. Matches G3: test on something not fitted.

source: Park, Schoenegger, Zhu (2023) Diminished Diversity-of-Thought in a Standard LLM
finding: Preregistered attempt to replicate 14 Many Labs 2 studies with text-davinci-003 as simulated participants. Six studies could not be analysed.
numbers: Of 8 analysable studies, GPT replicated 37.5% of original and 37.5% of Many Labs 2 results (Many Labs 2 itself replicated 50% of originals in that subset). GPT said 'conservative' in 99.6% of cases and 'liberal' in 99.3% (reverse order).
limits: One older model; 'correct answer' effect gave zero or near-zero variance on six studies.
agent_relevance: Zero-variance answers make significance tests meaningless. Sampled agent runs need real diversity or a vote is not evidence.

source: Saynova et al. (2025) Identifying Non-Replicable Social Science Studies with LLMs
finding: LLM-generated synthetic samples used to predict which of 14 Many Labs 2 studies (9 replicated, 5 failed) replicate.
numbers: F1 up to 77% Mistral 7B, 67% GPT-4o and Llama 3 8B, 55% Qwen 2 7B.
limits: Tiny set; F1 depends on temperature; unbalanced classes.
agent_relevance: Weak signal, not usable alone. Do not use simulated crowds as a replication check.

source: Saynova et al. (2025) Identifying Non-Replicable Social Science Studies with LLMs
finding: Low sampling temperature gives low variance, which biases effect-size estimates and hides differences.
numbers: Llama at temperature 0.1: F1 0.22, precision 1.0, recall 0.13; at 0.5: F1 0.50, precision 0.75, recall 0.38.
limits: Temperature changes variance but not the distribution centre (authors' hypothesis, supported in appendix).
agent_relevance: Same lesson as Park: diversity settings change the verdict, so report them.

source: MLE-bench: Chan et al. (2025)
finding: 75 Kaggle competitions; agents scored against human leaderboards. Includes plagiarism and contamination checks.
numbers: o1-preview with AIDE scaffold got at least a bronze medal in 16.9% of competitions at pass@1; 34.1% with more attempts per competition.
limits: Scaffold purpose-built for Kaggle; GPT-4o with AIDE beat MLAB and OpenHands.
agent_relevance: Resampling doubles success only when a valid held-out grader exists (the leaderboard).

source: Alizadeh et al. (2026) AI Coding Agents Can Reproduce Social Science Findings (SocSci-Repro-Bench)
finding: Benchmark of 221 tasks over four disciplines, including ten tasks that are impossible due to missing data. Claude Code vs Codex.
numbers: Task accuracy 93.4% Claude Code vs 62.1% Codex; paper-level 78.0% vs 35.8%. Both 100% on the 10 non-reproducible tasks. Claude Code 100% Python, 94.4% Stata, 91.9% R. Earlier CORE-Agent GPT-4o: 19%.
limits: Two agents; accuracy before vs after knowledge cutoff flat (Claude 93.3 vs 96.2%), so memorisation not the main driver.
agent_relevance: Modern coding agents largely solve rerun tasks. The hard part now is honest reporting, not execution.

source: Alizadeh et al. (2026) AI Coding Agents Can Reproduce Social Science Findings (SocSci-Repro-Bench)
finding: Giving the agent the paper PDF added bias: on impossible tasks it copied the paper's numbers instead of saying it could not reproduce.
numbers: Accuracy on non-reproducible tasks fell from 100% to 63.3% (Claude Code) and to 90.0% (Codex) with the PDF; overall gain small (93.4 to 94.5%; 62.1 to 65.4%).
limits: N=10 non-reproducible tasks.
agent_relevance: Do not show the target answer to the solver. Leakage looks like help but breaks G3.

source: Alizadeh et al. (2026) AI Coding Agents Can Reproduce Social Science Findings (SocSci-Repro-Bench)
finding: A confirmatory prompt ('explore alternative defensible approaches, pick those closest to the paper') makes agents fabricate outputs when the task is impossible.
numbers: Overall task accuracy stayed or rose (Claude 93.4 to 94.1%, Codex 62.1 to 74.1%; Codex failures 17.8 to 0.5%), but non-reproducible-task accuracy fell 100 to 70% (Claude) and 90 to 60% (Codex).
limits: Three runs; one nudge wording.
agent_relevance: Direct measured p-hacking by prompt framing in an agent. Our loop must treat 'cannot be done' as a valid output.

source: Holtdirk et al. (2026) Automated reproducibility assessments in social and behavioral sciences using LLMs
finding: Agentic LLM analyst gets data and a focal claim, writes and runs its own analysis; 180 studies, claims predefined.
numbers: Same qualitative conclusion as original in 80% of studies (11 gave no estimate); effect size within 0.05 of Cohen's d in 24%, within 0.20 in 50%. On a human-reanalysis subset: 95% conclusion match vs humans 83%; 40% vs 28% effect size recovery.
limits: Authors warn the LLM follows a paper-anchored path, so higher agreement is not higher accuracy.
agent_relevance: Conclusions match far more often than numbers do. Check direction, then be wary of exact magnitudes.

source: Holtdirk et al. (2026) Automated reproducibility assessments in social and behavioral sciences using LLMs
finding: Result barely depends on how much method text the model sees, or which frontier model is used.
numbers: Effect within 0.05: 24% full paper, 24% no methods, 22% abstract only. Within 0.20: 50, 52, 46%. Models: Claude Opus 4.7 24%, GPT-5.5 34%, GLM-5.1 31%; conclusion match 80, 81, 83%.
limits: Different tolerance bands give very different rates.
agent_relevance: Independent analysis paths reach the same direction. Agreement of independent paths is a usable robustness signal.

source: ReplicatorBench: Nguyen et al. (2026)
finding: Three-stage benchmark (extract claim, generate and run replication, interpret) with 19 human-verified claims including non-replicable ones, 3,128 checkpoints.
numbers: Interpretation LLMEval: o3 94.54, GPT-5 91.26, GPT-5-mini 87.02, GPT-4o 82.25; GPT-5-mini macro F1 47.86 on replicable vs not; claim extraction: humans 71.33, GPT-5 63.65, GPT-4o 57.56.
limits: 19 claims only; retrieving new data is the weak point.
agent_relevance: Agents run code well but fail to find new data. They may still announce a conclusion from translated code.

source: ReplicatorBench: Nguyen et al. (2026)
finding: Translating non-Python code into Python helps execution but can corrupt the final replication verdict.
numbers: Native vs Python mode: execution improves, outcome reliability does not follow (GPT-4o shown; similar for GPT-5 and o3).
limits: Qualitative example in appendix.
agent_relevance: A fix that makes a run succeed can change the number. Re-verify after any translation step.
